Parent initiative: #1985

## Problem

Robota has no reusable server-level MCP client or canonical capability catalog. The private `agent-tool-mcp` package calls a predeclared tool over a handwritten Streamable HTTP path, while `dag-node-mcp-tool` separately demonstrates the official SDK. Neither discovers a server's tools/prompts/resources nor composes them into `agent-cli`.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P0 — minimum product-reachable client vertical slice.** Configuration alone does not make any MCP capability callable. A correctly placed shared client plus Streamable HTTP is the first usable end-to-end path.

## Architecture placement

- Reclassify/rename the private `agent-tool-mcp` package into a shared lower MCP client package, or replace it and migrate/remove the old package explicitly.
- The shared package owns official-SDK protocol mechanics, server capabilities, canonical tools/prompts/resources catalogs, provenance, naming, and transport ports.
- `agent-framework` owns only generic dynamic-tool/session contracts; `agent-command` owns command effects; `agent-cli` only composes the concrete client manager and renders generic output.
- DAG and agent products are sibling consumers of the shared seam; neither product depends on the other.

## Acceptance criteria

- A deployable product/workspace manifest gains an intentional dependency edge to the shared MCP client owner.
- A configured Streamable HTTP server completes initialization and paginated discovery through the official MCP SDK seam.
- Tools, prompts, and resources each have a canonical typed catalog with server provenance, stable collision-safe naming, capability/version metadata, and explicit adopted/adapted/rejected product exposure.
- Discovered tools can be registered through the existing generic dynamic-tool/session contract; no MCP-only runtime bypass is added.
- `agent-cli` composes the manager without owning protocol, catalog, retry, or policy logic.
- HTTP URL admission reuses a safe network-boundary/SSRF policy.
- Deprecated SSE and custom WebSocket compatibility receive explicit AAR decisions. They are not treated as mandatory standard transports: the MCP standard transport baseline is stdio plus Streamable HTTP.
- Initialization, pagination, capability absence, name collisions, malformed server data, provenance, and one end-to-end scripted product path have tests.
- The old handwritten/predeclared-tool path is migrated, wrapped behind the canonical owner, or removed; two independent MCP client stacks cannot remain authoritative.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns HTTP, explicit SSE/WebSocket decisions, product composition, and initial discovery/catalog ownership for tools/prompts/resources. Refresh and last-known-good lifecycle are owned by the supervisor child.

## Non-goals and related issues

- Stdio process execution is a separate child.
- Connection retries/timeouts/state are a separate supervisor child.
- #1989 owns permission matching; #1990 owns tool-search and model-visible failed-server projection.
- #1986 owns exposing Robota as an MCP server.

## Moving references

Use the current [Claude Code MCP reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), [MCP transports specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports), and official capability specifications. Record a verdict for every capability/transport rather than copying one product.

- Add stdio as a transport adapter behind the shared MCP client transport port.
- Extract/reuse the official SDK seam at a shared lower owner; keep DAG and agent products as siblings.

Parent initiative: #1985

## Problem

No canonical owner maintains MCP connection state or discovered capability catalogs. The existing predeclared-tool HTTP code has limited per-attempt timeout/retry behavior but does not own server initialization, `list_changed`, last-known-good catalogs, reconnect state, discovery retries, or distinct timeout classes.

**P1 — connection/catalog state-machine foundation.** It is independently verifiable after the P0 client vertical slice and is required for reliable multi-server operation.

## Scope and ownership

- The shared MCP client package owns one supervisor per server and canonical state transitions.
- It produces structured pending/connected/failed/disabled state and capability catalogs.
- Existing #1990 alone owns projecting failed state to the model and tool-search path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Initialization and capability discovery classify transient, authentication, configuration, and not-found failures explicitly.
- Initial transient failures and discovery calls use bounded retry; auth/config/not-found failures are not blindly retried.
- Remote reconnect uses bounded exponential backoff with observable pending/failed/manual-retry states.
- Tool, prompt, and resource `list_changed` notifications refresh their catalog without reconnecting; a failed refresh preserves the prior last-known-good catalog and exposes stale/error metadata.
- Startup, per-server/per-call, global-default, and idle timeout semantics are distinct, configurable through typed settings, and tested.
- Cancellation and session shutdown cannot leave hidden live requests or reconnect loops.
- State transitions and retry timers are deterministic under a fake clock; no foreground polling or quiet failure.
- #1990 consumes the canonical failed state rather than deriving a second status model.
- Cache/persistence, if adopted, has explicit identity/invalidation and is not inferred from stale session data.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns `list_changed`, last-known-good refresh, reconnect/backoff, initial retry classification, discovery retry, pending/failed/manual retry, startup/per-server/global/idle timeouts. It supplies failed state to #1990 but does not own model projection.

Parent initiative: #1985

## Problem

Remote MCP servers commonly require OAuth. Robota has no MCP authorization flow, token store/clear lifecycle, protected-resource discovery, callback policy, client metadata override, scope restriction, or audience-bound token enforcement.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P1 — remote authorization protocol.** Broad remote-server interoperability requires it after the P0 HTTP foundation, and incorrect implementation risks credential disclosure.

## Scope and ownership

- Implement MCP remote authorization through a dedicated port behind the shared client package.
- Follow current MCP authorization requirements, including OAuth 2.1 security practices, PKCE, protected-resource metadata, audience binding, and secure storage.
- `agent-command` owns login/status/clear effects; UI only renders.

## Acceptance criteria

- OAuth authorization-code flow uses PKCE and validates state, redirect target, issuer/resource metadata, token audience, and TLS requirements.
- Protected-resource and authorization-server metadata discovery are bounded, validated, and protected against SSRF/redirect confusion.
- Fixed callback port, preconfigured client credentials, metadata overrides, and scope restriction are typed options with strict precedence and diagnostics.
- Access/refresh credentials are stored through a secure owner, keyed to the exact server/resource identity, never logged, and clearable/revocable.
- Refresh, expiry, invalid grant, reauthentication, cancellation, and partial-flow recovery are deterministic.
- Tokens cannot be sent to a different origin/resource through redirect, configuration change, or name collision.
- Tests use deterministic local fixtures for success, PKCE/state failure, metadata failure, audience mismatch, refresh, clear, cancellation, and redaction.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns OAuth command flow, credential storage/clearing, callback port, client credentials, metadata-discovery override, and scope restriction.

## Non-goals and related issues

- Does not execute dynamic header helper commands; that is a separate trust boundary.
- Does not let CLI code own token storage or protocol logic.

## Moving references

Use the current [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization) and [Claude Code MCP reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp). Record any product-specific adaptation explicitly.

Parent initiative: #1985

## Problem

Some non-OAuth servers need headers computed at connection time. A `headersHelper`-style feature executes a local command and turns its output into credentials, which is not an OAuth protocol concern: it introduces command trust, cwd/environment authority, timeout, output-bound, parsing, and redaction risks.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P2 — optional custom-auth execution surface.** It should not block standard HTTP/OAuth reachability and must not be smuggled into the OAuth gate.

## Scope and ownership

- Add an explicit opt-in dynamic-header provider behind the shared client authentication port.
- Reuse activation trust and subprocess authority primitives without reusing the stdio server process as an auth helper.
- Keep helper output ephemeral and narrowly scoped to one server connection attempt.

## Acceptance criteria

- A helper cannot run until workspace/source activation trust succeeds and the operator can identify the exact command authority.
- Command, args, cwd, and environment inheritance are typed and allowlisted; project content cannot silently broaden them.
- Execution has strict startup/wall-clock/output limits, cancellation, and process cleanup.
- Stdout is decoded by a strict JSON/header schema; duplicate/forbidden headers, non-string values, trailing junk, stderr confusion, and malformed output fail visibly.
- Helper output and derived headers are never printed, persisted in ordinary logs, or included in diagnostics; redaction covers failure paths.
- Results are scoped to the intended server identity and are not reused across a changed endpoint/configuration without an explicit cache contract.
- Tests cover untrusted source, denied command, env leakage, timeout, oversized output, malformed JSON, forbidden headers, cancellation, and redaction.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns only dynamic headers from a helper for custom authentication schemes.

## Non-goals and related issues

- Does not implement OAuth, token storage, or stdio MCP server transport.
- Does not make helper execution a default or prerequisite for ordinary static headers.

## Moving reference

Revalidate `headersHelper` behavior and trust requirements in the current [Claude Code MCP reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), then record a reasoned Robota AAR decision.

Parent initiative: #1985

## Problem

Third-party MCP tool input schemas may contain root `anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf` or other constructs rejected by a provider API. Dropping the whole server loses unrelated valid tools, while flattening without a provider-aware contract can misrepresent accepted input. CORE-040 validates runtime schemas but does not own model-facing provider projection.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P1 — provider-safe schema projection boundary.** A multi-provider MCP client needs explicit, testable projection rather than Anthropic-only rewriting or server-wide failure.

## Architecture placement

- Define a provider-neutral projection contract at the shared lower tool/provider boundary.
- Each provider package owns the strategy for its API constraints and declares unsupported behavior.
- Reuse CORE-040 runtime validation for untrusted schemas; do not create a second validator.

## Acceptance criteria

- Untrusted MCP schemas are validated before projection and cannot exploit prototype keys, cycles, unsupported references, or unbounded complexity.
- Provider strategies explicitly adopt, adapt, or reject root `anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf` and other unsupported keywords.
- When a safe semantic projection exists, the callable schema and explanatory description remain consistent and are deterministic.
- When projection is unsafe/impossible, only that tool is quarantined with a structured diagnostic; other tools and server capabilities remain available.
- Runtime argument validation remains against the authoritative original/normalized contract so projection cannot widen accepted execution input.
- Tool provenance and provider/model identity are part of projection diagnostics and cache identity.
- Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible, Gemini, and any other supported provider have explicit conformance tests or an explicit unsupported verdict.
- Fuzz/fixture tests cover combinators, nested/ref schemas, malformed input, one-invalid-tool isolation, and description consistency.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns root-combinator handling, provider-neutral mapping, and single-invalid-tool isolation.

## Non-goals and related issues

- Does not own discovery/catalog refresh or generic result-size admission.
- Does not preserve a legacy handwritten transformation merely to minimize migration.

## Moving references

Revalidate tool schema and invalid-tool behavior in the current [MCP tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools) and [Claude Code MCP reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), then record provider-specific AAR decisions.

Parent initiative: #1986

## Problem

`agent-transport-mcp` exposes `submit` and independently synthesized `command_*` tools, but it cannot list or invoke the session's canonical runtime tools. The framework already projects model-invocable commands as canonical `robota_command_*` runtime tools. The MCP path therefore gives commands a second identity and execution path and cannot expose ordinary agent tools without bypassing session policy.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P0 — canonical runtime-capability boundary.** A product server must not become reachable until every direct MCP tool call uses the same permission, hook, result, truncation, event, audit, and cancellation path as normal session execution.

## Architecture ownership

- `agent-interface-session` owns a provider-neutral `ISessionRuntimeTools`-like list/invoke capability.
- `agent-session` and `agent-framework` implement/expose it over the existing permission-wrapped runtime.
- `agent-transport-mcp` translates that capability to MCP tools; it does not reach into a tool manager or implement policy.
- Existing #2091 and #2107 own bound-adapter lifecycle and exact MCP/session-port attachment. This issue supplies the final narrow runtime-tool capability that #2107 binds.

## Acceptance criteria

- The narrow session port lists every canonical runtime tool with its existing name, description, and validated input schema.
- Invocation by canonical name goes through one session-owned method preserving permission decisions, pre/post hooks, execution events/audit, result envelope, truncation/output admission, errors, and provider-neutral cancellation.
- MCP cancellation maps to the port's `AbortSignal`/cancellation contract and cannot leave an unobserved execution.
- Concurrency semantics are explicit for concurrent MCP calls, direct tool calls versus `submit`, queueing, cancellation, and session shutdown.
- Projected commands appear only as `robota_command_*`; the parallel `command_*` catalog and direct `executeCommand` path are removed without a compatibility shim.
- Retained `submit` is documented as a Robota extension, uses a reserved collision-safe identity, and fails startup if a collision cannot be resolved safely.
- A direct call requiring interactive permission fails closed with a visible MCP tool error when the host has no approved noninteractive policy.
- Prompts and resources are explicitly unsupported in the minimum slice until canonical runtime registries with their distinct control semantics exist.
- In-memory MCP tests cover canonical listing/invocation, command identity, denied/ask/allowed policy, hooks, truncation, cancellation, concurrency, collision, unknown tools, and one-tool failure isolation.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns exposure of the agent's own tools, preservation of server-side permissions, and the tools/resources/prompts disposition.

## Dependencies and ordering

- C1 and #2091 can execute independently.
- Both must complete before #2107 binds the exact MCP capability port.
- The stdio product child depends on #2107.
- #1989 may later enrich generic permission grammar but is not a blocker for preserving current fail-closed policy.

## Non-goals

- Does not connect stdio/HTTP carriers or add a CLI process mode.
- Does not invent prompt/resource registries for parity.
- Does not keep a prerelease duplicate command identity for compatibility.

## Moving references

Record adopted/adapted/rejected decisions against the current [Claude Code MCP server reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) and [MCP tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools). Robota intentionally keeps stronger server-side policy even though the reference client also owns user confirmation.

Parent initiative: #1986

## Problem

The public MCP server builder is not a deployable product mode. `createMcpTransport.start()` creates an MCP `Server` object but does not connect a carrier, and `agent-cli` has no `mcp serve` route. A local-looking CLI call to the raw SDK would duplicate carrier lifecycle and make an incomplete surface reachable.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P0 — minimum carrier-owning product vertical slice.** This is the first user-reachable server path after the canonical runtime-tool port and exact adapter binding are complete.

## Architecture ownership

- `agent-transport-mcp` owns `StdioServerTransport`, connect/readiness/close semantics, and protocol translation.
- `agent-cli` owns only the `robota mcp serve` process-mode selection, normal product/session composition, cwd/trust posture, stdout/stderr/signals/exit behavior, and bundled dependency arrangement.
- `agent-command` does not own this process mode.

## Acceptance criteria

- `robota mcp serve` starts exactly one normal Robota session and connects it to one official SDK stdio carrier.
- Transport readiness means the carrier is connected and able to serve requests, not merely that a `Server` object exists.
- The MCP package owns carrier close/idempotency/error semantics; CLI code does not import the raw MCP SDK to recreate them.
- The process inherits the caller-selected working directory through the normal project-root/access/trust boundary.
- Stdout is reserved exclusively for MCP protocol frames from process start through shutdown; banners, logs, progress, warnings, and diagnostics go to stderr or a non-stdout sink.
- SIGINT/SIGTERM, stdin close, client disconnect, startup failure, active request cancellation, and normal exit have deterministic cleanup and exit codes.
- The published/bundled CLI contains the required MCP implementation without an unresolved workspace-only runtime edge.
- A real binary-level test launches the CLI, connects an MCP client over stdio, lists canonical tools, invokes one allowed tool, observes one denied/ask failure, and shuts down cleanly.
- User documentation provides the exact host configuration, executable resolution, working-directory semantics, exposed surface, security model, and troubleshooting.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns the single-command stdio server, caller-controlled working directory, and documentation of the served surface.

## Dependencies and ordering

- Blocked by #2107, which in turn requires this initiative's canonical-runtime-tool child and existing #2091.
- #2117 is downstream cleanup and does not block this product slice.

- Does not add Streamable HTTP, multi-session addressing, or remote authentication.
- Does not use the generic human headless host issue #2087 as an MCP carrier.

Parent initiative: #1986

## Problem

Remote MCP hosting needs a standard Streamable HTTP carrier plus an explicit mapping between protocol connections and Robota runtime sessions. Reusing `agent-transport-http` or `agent-transport-ws` would be incorrect because they carry Robota protocols, not MCP. Even loopback is a hostile network boundary in this repository.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P2/security — optional authenticated local HTTP carrier and session-addressing boundary.** It follows the stdio product slice and cannot be released non-loopback until the remote authorization child lands.

## Architecture ownership

- `agent-transport-mcp` owns the official Streamable HTTP carrier and protocol-session mapping.
- Reuse the shared network admission primitive; do not fork URL/Host/Origin/token policy inside CLI code.
- `Mcp-Session-Id` is a protocol-session mapping key, not a Robota session ID and never an authentication credential.

## Acceptance criteria

- Streamable HTTP implements the current MCP transport requirements, including POST/GET/session lifecycle and protocol-version behavior adopted by the design.
- The first release binds loopback only and requires an auto-minted, high-entropy bearer credential or equivalently strong shared admission; unauthenticated loopback is rejected.
- Host and Origin are strictly validated before request/body processing, with DNS rebinding/alternate-host tests.
- Protocol session identifiers are unguessable mapping keys bound server-side to the intended Robota runtime session and credential context; they cannot authorize access by themselves.
- Single/multiple runtime-session policy, creation/selection, concurrency, cancellation, resumption, expiry, disconnect, and shutdown are explicit and bounded.
- C1 remains the owner of transport-neutral execution/cancellation semantics; the carrier only projects wire events.
- Logs and errors redact bearer/session material and cannot leak response bodies or internal runtime IDs.
- Real HTTP tests cover valid/invalid Host, Origin, bearer, session mapping, concurrent requests, cancellation/resume, expiry, disconnect, and shutdown.
- Non-loopback binding is mechanically refused until the remote authorization capability is present and configured.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns non-stdio standard transport and session addressing/multi-session decisions.

## Dependencies

- Blocked by the stdio product child because it establishes the carrier abstraction and canonical server surface.
- Blocks the remote resource-server authorization child; that child in turn blocks all non-loopback release.

## Non-goals

- Does not implement custom MCP WebSocket transport.
- Does not reuse Robota HTTP/WS protocol adapters as MCP carriers.
- Does not treat `Mcp-Session-Id` as auth.

## Moving reference

Revalidate and record AAR decisions from the current [MCP Streamable HTTP transport specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports).

Parent initiative: #1986

## Problem

Exposing the MCP server beyond loopback requires resource-server authorization and admission. Client OAuth issue #2526 acquires credentials for Robota as a client; it does not validate tokens, audience, scopes, or access when Robota is the protected MCP resource.

## Recommended priority and cause

**P2/security — remote protected-resource boundary.** It blocks every non-loopback Streamable HTTP release but is independent of local stdio and authenticated loopback reachability.

## Architecture ownership

- Place generic token-verifier/scope/admission ports in the repository's designated auth owner.
- `agent-transport-mcp` owns MCP protected-resource metadata/challenges and maps validated claims to runtime/session admission.
- Product composition selects concrete verifier/storage/network adapters; CLI does not validate tokens itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- Publish standards-compliant protected-resource metadata and `WWW-Authenticate` challenges without leaking internal topology.
- Validate issuer, signature/algorithm, expiry/not-before, audience/resource, scopes, token type, and replay-relevant identity before session lookup or request execution.
- Token audience/scope is bound to the exact MCP resource and authorized operations; a valid client token for another resource is rejected.
- Authentication and authorization failures are rate-limited/audited with redacted diagnostics and do not reveal whether a runtime session exists.
- Session mapping remains separate from authentication; `Mcp-Session-Id` alone grants no authority.
- Key/metadata refresh, verifier outage, clock skew, revocation/expiry, malformed challenges, cancellation, and shutdown fail closed.
- Tests cover valid access, missing/invalid token, wrong audience/scope/resource, expired/not-yet-valid token, algorithm confusion, metadata failure, rate limiting, redaction, and session-enumeration resistance.
- A mechanical gate prevents non-loopback bind/release unless this admission capability is configured.

## Parent checklist ownership

Owns authentication and authorization for non-stdio MCP server transports.

## Dependencies and related issues

- Blocked by the Streamable HTTP/session-addressing child.
- #2526 remains the separate MCP client OAuth owner and must not be reused as this implementation item.

## Non-goals

- Does not acquire client credentials or implement authorization-code UI.
- Does not weaken authenticated loopback admission owned by the HTTP carrier child.

## Moving reference

Use the current [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization) and record product-specific AAR decisions before implementation.
